newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Western powers devise new Bosnia returnees plan.
newsitem.headline: Western powers devise new Bosnia returnees plan.

text.p: International agencies in Bosnia on Tuesday presented a new plan to overcome a crisis surrounding the return of refugees to homes they were forced to leave during 43 months of war.

Michael Steiner of Germany, deputy head of the office charged with the reconstruction of Bosnia, said people wanting to rebuild and reoccupy houses located in ethnic flashpoints would be able to apply to an international commission.
They would be allowed to go ahead if they could prove they owned the houses and were not serving members of the armed forces or police.
Rebuilding work would be aided by cash from the European Commission, which had substantial funds at its disposal, Steiner said.
"The aim is that we transform the Zone of Separation into a zone of cooperation," Steiner told a news conference.
"Whether it will work will depend on the willingness of the parties to play the game. It is a balanced approach."

The resettlement of villagers in the demilitarised Zone of Separation that runs along the wartime front line has become fraught with fear and mistrust, turning villages in northern Bosnia into security flashpoints.

Moslems accuse Serbs of blowing up houses they are trying to rebuild in Serb territory, while Serbs accuse Moslems of violating the zone by bringing in arms banned under the December 1995 Dayton peace accord.
NATO officials reported renewed tension at the northern Bosnian village of Jusici, where Moslems have resettled homes in an area held by the Serbs.

Steiner said the new plan had been agreed by the Office of the High Representative, of which he is deputy head, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the NATO peacekeeping force, the U.N. police task force and the EU Commission.
Moslem, Serb and Croat officials had been presented with the plan at a meeting in Sarajevo, Steiner said, adding that the international community had the power to impose it without consultation.
Thousands of displaced people would be able to take advantage of the scheme, but with the approach of winter likely to slow rebuilding work, the process could take some time.

In northern Bosnia, tension mounted in Jusici, where about 50 Serbs demonstrated at a checkpoint manned by NATO peacekeeping forces, saying it was too far from the village and would allow Moslems to infiltrate surrounding areas.
"Such demonstrations ratchet up tension and increase the chances of violent incident," NATO spokesman Major Simon Haselock said.
